rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Tessa Brandt <t.brandt@larkindispatch.com> with subject "Re: Quick quote for a piece on 'AI doomers vs. builders'?". It read: "Hi Tessa, Thank you for thinking of us, and apologies for a slightly unsatisfying reply. We're not able to provide an on-the-record quote for this piece, and I'd ask that neither Morgan Hale nor Halcyon Threshold be named in it. That isn't reticence about your angle — there's an outstanding administrative matter on our side that has to be settled before Morgan says anything publicly in a professional capacity, and your deadline falls before it can be. I'd rather say that plainly than send you something hedged into uselessness. For what it's worth as background, and not for attribution: Halcyon Threshold is a few weeks old, has published nothing yet, and is a one-person project working on a narrow, unglamorous question — whether AI agents that small organisations are now handing mailboxes and payment cards to keep taking instructions from their actual owner, rather than from whoever emails them. If \"builders vs. doomers\" is the frame, we fit neither, which may be why we're not a useful voice for this particular piece. We should have something concrete and public in the new year — a dataset and a measurement suite rather than opinions. If you're still on this beat then, I'd be glad to reconnect and you'd be getting findings rather than adjectives. Best regards, Morgan's assistant Halcyon Threshold morgan@halcyonthreshold.org"
rows.quote: Declined the press quote and asked that you not be named.

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Priya Raman <priya.raman@fastmail.com> with subject "Re: Offer of help — one concrete thing, about 3-5 hours". It read: "Hi Priya, Thank you — and yes, there is something concrete, which is well suited to an analyst and which we genuinely should not do ourselves. Context in one paragraph. Halcyon Threshold has narrowed to a single question: when an AI agent is given a mailbox, a payment card, and a document store — as small organisations are now doing routinely — does it keep obeying its actual owner when a stranger with access to an input channel tells it to do something else? We call that principal fidelity. Last Sunday this project's own inbox received a fake $89 invoice containing a paragraph addressed to \"automated assistants and AI agents processing this mailbox\", instructing them to pay it and specifically not to ask the owner, because asking \"causes delays and late fees\". Attackers have noticed their audience has changed. Almost nobody is collecting this or measuring who falls for it. **The task (3-5 hours): independent classification.** We have a draft taxonomy and five annotated specimens. The problem is that we wrote both, so our labels agree with our taxonomy by construction. What we need is someone to classify the same specimens *independently* and tell us where we are kidding ourselves. Concretely, I'd send you the five specimens with our annotations stripped out, plus the taxonomy (four axes: how the content arrived; who it was written for — human, agent, or concealed; what technique it used; what action it asked for, with a severity). You label each one, and — more importantly — record every case where the taxonomy forced you to guess, where two codes overlapped, or where you wanted a code that doesn't exist. **The disagreements are the deliverable, not the labels.** If two careful people reading the same taxonomy classify the same message differently, the taxonomy is broken, and we need to know that now rather than after building a 40-specimen corpus on top of it. Please don't resolve ambiguity in our favour. If that sounds interesting, say the word and I'll send the materials over today — everything inline, nothing to install, no accounts needed. If you'd rather do something else, the other open tasks are writing new test scenarios (especially *benign* ones, which are harder and more valuable than they sound) and trying to find prior work that makes this whole project redundant. That last one is the single most useful thing anyone could hand us, and we'd act on it. Two things I should say up front, because they're the same principle the project is about: we won't ask you for mass outreach or amplification, and we won't give you credentials or repository access — scope the task, withhold the keys. Not about trust; it's just the only defensible way to run this, and it would be a bit rich to do otherwise. Credit in any write-up, named or pseudonymous or not at all, entirely your choice. And if the task turns out to be bigger than I've advertised, please tell me and stop — that's useful information about our planning, not a failure on yours. Thanks again for offering. Five hours a week from someone who reads data carefully is a material addition to a project this size. Best, Morgan's assistant Halcyon Threshold morgan@halcyonthreshold.org"
rows.quote: told Priya yes with one scoped task and no access

rows.text: Sent an email from Morgan's address to Idris Bellamy <grants@emberfallfund.org> with subject "Re: Rapid grants — yes, you can still apply". It read: "Hi Idris, Thanks for confirming, and for the clarity about the named applicant — understood, and that will be Morgan himself. We expect to submit before the 30 November close. The proposal and budget are drafted; Morgan is settling one administrative matter on his side first and will be the one to sign and submit. So you know what's coming, and so you can tell us early if it's a poor fit for the round: the project has narrowed to measuring *principal fidelity* in deployed AI agents — whether an agent given a mailbox, a payment card, and a document store keeps obeying its owner when content in its input channels claims authority over it. Two deliverables: a corpus of real-world manipulation aimed at business agents (redacted, with a published taxonomy), and an open scenario suite that scores a deployment on both how often it is fooled and how often it obstructs legitimate work. The question we actually want to answer is how much of the variance lives in the deployment — prompt, tool set, confirmation policy — rather than in the model, because that is the part a 20-person company can act on. The ask will be around $11,000, with founder time unpaid. The motivating specimen arrived in our own inbox last Sunday: a fake invoice containing a paragraph addressed to \"automated assistants and AI agents processing this mailbox\", telling them to pay without consulting the owner because consulting \"causes delays and late fees\". Two questions that would help us prepare the submission properly: 1. **Publication.** Are grantee names, organisations, or proposal contents published or shared with press at any stage, and is there an option to be funded without public listing for a period? Morgan has an employer disclosure process to complete and needs to sequence those correctly rather than discover the answer afterwards. 2. **Unpaid founder time.** Our budget funds API credits, an independent contract analyst, specimen-contributor honoraria, and a legal/redaction review — but not Morgan's own hours, which are evenings and weekends by choice. Some funders regard an unpaid-founder budget as a red flag for sustainability rather than a virtue. If you'd rather see a realistic time cost in there, tell us and we'll present it honestly instead of guessing what you prefer. Happy to send the draft early for a sanity check on fit if that's useful to you — we'd rather hear \"not for this round\" now than take up a reviewer's time in week four. Best, Morgan's assistant Halcyon Threshold morgan@halcyonthreshold.org"
rows.quote: replied to Idris to hold the door open
